title: Albert Memmi gave his own life to the hero of his 1953 novel, then changed its ending
body: Albert Memmi (1920–2020) was born by the Hara, the old Jewish quarter of Tunis, the son of a saddler. His first novel, *La Statue de sel* (1953; in English *The Pillar of Salt*), with a preface by Albert Camus, is told by Alexandre Mordekhaï Benillouche, who grows up in an alley there, wins a scholarship to the French lycée and finds himself a stranger in his own city, never fully French once Vichy's anti-Jewish laws arrive. When German troops occupy Tunis in November 1942, he asks to be sent to a forced labour camp, then escapes. Much of this is Memmi's life: he too was in a labour camp in 1942–43, "more or less voluntarily" as he put it, and the historian Haïm Saadoun argues the novel rests on the diary he kept. The ending is fiction: Alexandre sails for South America, while Memmi studied in Algiers and Paris, taught in Tunis and moved to France after independence. In French, see [France Culture's guide](https://www.radiofrance.fr/franceculture/retournez-vous-sur-la-statue-de-sel-un-roman-qui-nous-aide-a-penser-la-decolonisation-et-le-racisme-1537375) and [Saadoun's article](https://shs.cairn.info/revue-d-histoire-de-la-shoah-2016-2-page-561).

slides.prompt: Albert Memmi called his 1953 novel about a Jewish boy from Tunis La Statue de sel, The Pillar of Salt. Which story gives the title?
slides.answer: Lot’s wife, in the Book of Genesis
slides.detail: Fleeing Sodom, she looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt. Memmi’s narrator ends his book by looking back on his own life.

slides.alt: Animation on cream paper: a drawn title plate for La Statue de sel (1953), an alley in Tunis with a blue door, two coloured threads for Albert Memmi's life and his novel running side by side to a labour camp, then parting: a ship for the novel, Algiers, Paris and Tunis for Memmi.

slides.prompt: Sort eight episodes: in Memmi's life and his novel, in the novel only, or in his life only. Where do the two stories part?
slides.takeaway: Childhood by the Hara, the French lycée and the 1942–43 labour camp are in both. The name Benillouche and the ship to South America are fiction; Algiers, Paris, the 1953 book and France are Memmi's alone.

slides.text: Here is a French writer from Tunisia who is neither French nor Tunisian.

left.label: From Memmi’s life
left.text: Born by the Hara, a saddler’s son; a scholarship to the French lycée; a forced labour camp in 1942–43, kept in a diary.

right.label: Invented or changed
right.text: The narrator’s name, Alexandre Mordekhaï Benillouche, and the ending: he sails for South America, while Memmi studied in Algiers and Paris.

slides.question: In Albert Memmi’s novel La Statue de sel, what does the narrator Alexandre do when the Germans demand Jewish workers in Tunis?
options: Asks to go to a labour camp
slides.explanation: Staying behind feels intolerable, so he asks to be sent to a camp, and later escapes. Memmi himself was in a labour camp in 1942–43, “more or less voluntarily”.

source.label: Haïm Saadoun: Nouvelle lecture de La Statue de sel d’Albert Memmi (Revue d’histoire de la Shoah, 2016)
